strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: mismatch between VLM generative outputs (multiple valid interpretations) and exact-match HOI evaluation protocols that unfairly penalize both VLMs and methods, particularly underestimating VLM performance

Comprehensive benchmark design with intelligent multi-stage construction: VLM-based filtering with cross-validation (GPT-4.1 → Qwen2.5-VL → GPT-4o), test set redistribution (KL divergence 0.088→0.629), and manual hard-case refinement emphasizing multi-person scenarios (38.9% vs 7.5% in HICO-DET)
Three complementary evaluation settings (1: all persons; 2: target person with box; 3: detection + recognition) that capture different task aspects and address annotation sparsity issues

Rigorous experimental evaluation with diverse baselines (7 VLMs of varying sizes, 5 HOI-specific methods), multiple metrics (Macro-F1, Instance-F1, Micro-F1, EM), and detailed error analysis with qualitative examples revealing actionable insights about VLM limitations in multi-person scenarios and detection

Clear, well-motivated findings: VLMs struggle to disentangle target person from surrounding individuals (20-25% error rate), detection is a major bottleneck (16.6% Instance-F1 drop from Setting 2→3), while large VLMs exceed HOI-specific methods in recognition

Excellent presentation with well-designed examples (frisbee/airplane ambiguity), comprehensive comparisons with existing benchmarks (Table 1), detailed implementation details, and 68 time-sensitive ambiguous HOI classes identified
Practical design choices including human-centric formulation, randomized 4-choice format addressing LLM positional bias, and support for multiple correct answers reflecting real-world ambiguity
weaknesses: Small dataset scale (1,274 images, ~13% of original HICO-DET test set) raises concerns about statistical significance and generalization; no confidence intervals, significance tests, or cross-validation results reported; inter-annotator agreement statistics absent

Potential circularity in benchmark construction: Qwen2.5-VL-32B used in negative choice filtering pipeline while being a baseline (achieves highest performance at 63.16% Macro-F1), despite cross-checking with GPT-4o—unclear if benchmark design biases results toward this model

Limited to HICO-DET only with no validation on V-COCO, SWiG-HOI, or other HOI datasets; generalization of findings across different domains and distributions unknown, reducing applicability for future research

Methodological inconsistencies: top-5 matching for HOI-specific methods vs. natural multi-output VLMs introduces fairness concerns; manual refinement criteria (defining 'obviously simple' vs. 'challenging') lack formal specification and potential annotator bias not discussed

Incomplete analysis of multiple correct answers: identifies 68 ambiguous classes but doesn't quantify distribution of answer set sizes across settings or characterize how multiple-answer prevalence affects evaluation fairness

Detection evaluation design concerns: Setting 3 with VLM-based detection shows poor results, but Table 6 using external DETR detector partially sidesteps the issue; unclear how to best evaluate end-to-end VLM capabilities when detection is weak

Limited statistical rigor with no confidence intervals despite small dataset size; differences between models (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B: 51.29% vs Qwen2-VL-7B: 41.92%) lack statistical validation; fine-tuning experiments show no error bars or multiple runs

Reproducibility gaps: exact prompts for GPT-4.1 negative filtering not provided, manual refinement criteria not formally codified, data/code release plan mentioned but not detailed, and disagreement resolution process for manual curation unclear
Benchmark design primarily addresses task reformulation rather than introducing new methods or theoretical insights; technical novelty limited to multiple-choice reformulation with curated negatives

Missing analyses: limited investigation into root causes of VLM failures in multi-person scenarios beyond confirming they occur; no ablation studies on design choices (choice count, negative sampling); no comparison with alternative evaluation frameworks (e.g., open-ended generation with human judges)

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies real limitations of HICO-DET regarding incomplete annotations, ambiguous temporal actions (68 classes), and sparse multi-person labels that systematically underestimate VLM performance

Thoughtful benchmark design: Multiple-choice reformulation elegantly handles ambiguity while avoiding unbounded outputs; three complementary evaluation settings progressively test different task aspects; curated negatives through multi-stage VLM pipeline (GPT-4.1→Qwen→GPT-4o); increased proportion of challenging multi-person cases (38.9% vs 7.5%)

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Tests 7 VLMs and 5 HOI methods systematically with multiple metrics (Macro/Instance/Micro-F1, EM); detailed implementation details including per-model bounding box handling; fine-tuning analysis revealing class imbalance

Concrete, actionable findings: Large VLMs surpass HOI methods in recognition (+16.65% Macro-F1); VLMs weak at detection (16.6% Instance-F1 drop Setting 2→3); 20-25% errors from misattributing surrounding people's interactions; findings clearly delineate VLM strengths vs weaknesses

Dataset construction rigor: KL divergence analysis quantifying train-test similarity; manual refinement excluding trivial cases and adding hard negatives; 68 time-sensitive ambiguous classes identified
weaknesses: Significant dataset size reduction without statistical validation: Test set reduced from 9,658 to 1,274 images (~13% of original); no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; no analysis of whether 1,274 is statistically sufficient across HOI categories; raises generalizability concerns

Uneven evaluation comparison across paradigms: Top-5 matching for HOI-specific methods vs zero-shot for VLMs creates methodological asymmetry potentially inflating HOI scores; 4-choice format appears arbitrary without justification (why not 3/5/open-ended); may underutilize VLM capabilities

Limited negative choice validation: Using Qwen2.5-VL in both construction pipeline and as baseline creates potential bias despite GPT-4o cross-checking; 4-choice format inherently limits scope vs open-vocabulary HOI; no systematic validation that curated negatives are definitively negative; no inter-annotator agreement metrics for manual refinement stage

Insufficient analysis of multi-answer design: Minimal documentation of how frequently questions have multiple answers; no annotation agreement assessment; no ablation on impact of allowing vs prohibiting multiple answers; quality metrics for manual refinement stage absent

Limited novelty and prescriptive guidance: Primarily benchmarking contribution without new methods; findings identify problems (VLM detection weakness) without solutions; Table 6 using external DETR feels like workaround; no clear guidance for practitioners on using VLMs for end-to-end HOI detection

Incomplete training data treatment: 111,459 training questions modest vs VLM pretraining scale; long-tail distribution acknowledged but unaddressed; Figure 3 shows persistent class imbalance after fine-tuning with no proposed solution; no ablation on training data impact

Missing critical experiments: No ablation on hard negatives vs easy negatives; no cross-dataset generalization analysis; no inter-annotator agreement reported; no ablation on number-of-choices impact; missing results for some models (LLaVA-OV, small VLMs in Table 4)

Absent statistical rigor: No error bars or confidence intervals; no significance testing or p-values; unclear if results from single runs; small test set (1,274) makes strong conclusions uncertain; performance varies significantly across models (Qwen2-VL-7B: 41.92% vs Qwen2.5-VL-32B: 63.16% in Setting 1)

Reproducibility and validation gaps: Benchmark release postponed at submission; VLM prompting variations could significantly affect results; manual refinement stage details sparse (annotator count? agreement metrics?); no inter-annotator agreement for ground-truth annotations

Detection evaluation incomplete: Large VLMs substantially weaker at detection but paper acknowledges without solving; external DETR improvement (Table 6) raises fairness concerns; Setting 3 with specified target person not fully realistic; no guidance on practical VLM deployment

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations of existing HOI benchmarks (incomplete annotations, exact-match evaluation) with clear concrete examples
Elegant and practical multiple-choice QA reformulation that enables fair evaluation of both VLMs and HOI-specific methods while reducing annotation burden
Rigorous dataset construction with two-stage approach (coarse VLM screening + manual refinement) and strong validation (Table 4 shows HOI-specific models agree with negatives more than VLMs)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 7 VLM variants, 5 HOI methods, 3 benchmarks, detailed failure analysis, significance testing, and extensive supplementary ablations
Key empirical findings revealing complementary strengths/weaknesses: VLMs competitive at zero-shot reasoning (52.94% vs 47.76%) but weak at detection and multi-action recognition
Well-designed complementary evaluation settings (Settings 1-3) that isolate different aspects (detection, recognition, multi-person reasoning) while avoiding false negatives
Thoughtful bias mitigation: addresses circular Qwen bias (Table 12), position bias (Table 6), validates coarse screening doesn't favor VLMs, high inter-annotator agreement (95.22%)
Strong reproducibility: detailed implementation details, prompts, dataset construction methodology, proper licensing, and comprehensive supplementary materials
weaknesses: Dataset scale reduction from 9,546 to 1,274 images (~13%) raises statistical stability concerns; manual removal of 'simple' cases is somewhat subjective without formal criteria

MCQA format is pragmatic but represents substantial simplification from open-set evaluation (4 choices vs. 600 HOI classes); acknowledged but underemphasized limitation of assessing full generative capabilities

Limited analysis of benchmark characteristics: missing distribution of multi-label questions, no correlation of task difficulty with number of correct answers, no breakdown of which interactions are hardest

Evaluation gaps: some VLMs produce no valid boxes (Table 1), detector-assisted results show 6-19% improvements (Table 9) but relegated to supplementary, suggesting detection bottleneck more severe than main results indicate

Coarse screening validation incomplete: no analysis of VLM ensemble disagreement rates, Qwen bias validation only on 12% subset (Table 12), high agreement doesn't guarantee negatives are truly invalid
Sub-benchmark generalization concerns: large performance drops on V-COCO (18+) and SWiG-HOI (37+) suggest main benchmark findings may not generalize; V-COCO class mapping between datasets is complex
Some findings are somewhat predictable: VLM weakness in detection and multi-action recognition aligns with known limitations; limited insights into architectural/training modifications needed
Missing actionable improvements: paper identifies weaknesses but provides limited direction for enhancing either paradigm; no comparison of alternative reformulations (ranking, semantic similarity)

strengths: Well-motivated solution to real benchmark limitation: clearly articulates why exact-match evaluation under incomplete annotations unfairly penalizes VLMs and valid unlabeled predictions

Rigorous benchmark construction with multi-stage validation: coarse screening by multiple VLMs (99% vs 95-97% agreement in Table 4) plus manual refinement with high inter-annotator agreement (95.22% pairwise, 91% unanimous)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: three complementary settings isolate different capabilities; multiple metrics (Macro/Instance/Micro-F1, EM); bootstrap statistical significance testing; detailed failure case analysis

Valuable empirical insights about paradigm trade-offs: VLMs show strong contextual reasoning but struggle with multi-action recognition (54% of failures) and cross-person attribution (20-25%); HOI-specific methods excel at action recognition but lack general reasoning
Thorough reproducibility documentation: extensive supplementary material with prompts, implementation details, ablations, and dataset construction rationale enabling community reproduction
Confirmed difficulty increase: 8-12 point performance drop vs. full HICO-DET validates benchmark challenges real scenarios
Multiple evaluation sub-benchmarks provide complementary analysis: V-COCO for multi-person scenarios, SWiG-HOI for human-human interactions, revealing different generalization patterns
weaknesses: Circular bias inadequately addressed: Qwen2.5-VL-32B used in coarse screening AND evaluated as baseline; Table 12 ablation uses only 12% subset as evidence; should exclude Qwen variants entirely from screening or use independent models

Problematic VLM evaluation results with limited investigation: Qwen3-VL-30B shows 0.25% Instance-F1 with 100% Avg. Prec. (nonsensical); LLaVA-OV-7B and Qwen2-VL-7B produce no valid boxes; Qwen2.5-VL-32B drops 12.2 points Setting 1→2; insufficient analysis of failure causes raises protocol fairness concerns

Detection bottleneck fundamentally undermines VLM competitiveness claims: large VLMs drop 20+ points from Setting 2 (provided boxes) to Setting 1 (realistic detection); external DETR detector required for competitive performance; 'superior performance' claim applies mainly to unrealistic Setting 2 scenario

Multiple-choice format limits scope and claims: MCQA is easier than open-set generation, can only select from 4 options vs. infinite HOI space; requires ad-hoc text-to-choice mapping; treated as 'diagnostic' but implies real-world HOI understanding is overstated

Small test set (1,274 images vs. ~10K in HICO-DET) raises statistical power concerns despite comprehensive supplementary evaluation; some classes have very small sample sizes; confidence intervals show ±2% uncertainty

Incomplete analysis of negative curation robustness: 54.10% of negatives manually updated but agreement resolution not detailed; manual refinement could introduce subtle biases; Table 4 validates coarse-screened negatives but not manual refinements

Setting 2 design unfairly advantages VLMs: providing ground-truth boxes is unrealistic; only 2/5 HOI methods can use them; makes direct paradigm comparison impossible; justification for diagnostic setting is weak

Generalization challenges underexplored: fine-tuned VLMs exhibit head-class bias (Fig. 14b); V-COCO causes 7+ point Macro-F1 drop (62.90%→55.61%); SWiG-HOI drops further to 52.74%; limited analysis of distribution shift causes

Limited methodological novelty: contribution is benchmarking rather than proposing new methods or theoretical insights; compressed HOI-method performance (43-48% range) suggests insufficient discrimination or limited scope
